verdict.reasoning: Patient says symptoms started “maybe about two months or so… and that's probably coincides with me starting a new job… quite stressful,” indicating anxiety for ~2 months associated with starting a new retail job.

Patient states she gets “really nervous every morning about leaving the house” and at work is “really worried about whether I'm doing well or not,” consistent with morning nervousness, dread leaving the house, and worry about work performance.

She reports difficulty falling asleep: “I can't get to sleep for hours and hours and hours… I'm lying awake all night,” waking with racing heart: “I find my heart kind of racing… I find myself waking up before [the alarm],” and estimates “maybe three, four hours I'm getting now… even when I'm in sleep, it's such a shallow sleep.”

Palpitations: “Irregular, I think… it can be anything… a couple of minutes or… 10 minutes.” Location/time: “usually… in the morning… when I realize… I'm going to be late.” Chest discomfort: when asked about chest pain she answers, “No. Well, yeah, it's painful when… my heart is beating fast,” implying pain only during palpitations and no separate chest pain otherwise.

Low energy and anhedonia: “It's just really, really low… I find no enjoyment at all… anything that previously was really fun is just not enjoyable.” Social withdrawal: “I avoid [friends]… I know that I'm not going to have fun because I don't want to go out.” Exercise: “I did used to like to go running and to play tennis… but now… I'm not going out to do that quite so much,” consistent with decreased exercise (though not completely stopped).

She states: “Has it ever got so bad that you've actually had to miss work? Patient: No… But I do pretty much every morning I think, oh, I should call in sick,” confirming no missed work but frequent thoughts of calling in sick.

Regarding public transport she says, “I find public transport really stressful in a way, especially being on the tube because it's… really airless,” indicating anxiety is worse on public transport, particularly the tube.
When asked about prior similar times she replies, “Not really, no… I've never felt anything that's bad before,” supporting no prior similar episodes of anxiety.

On suicidal thoughts: “I haven't had any suicidal thoughts or any thoughts that have been that extreme… I don't have worries about actually wanting to not go on,” indicating denial of suicidality; she describes being “a bit down, a bit unhappy” but not extreme mood symptoms.

She states alcohol use is mainly on weekends: “probably quite a lot on the Friday or Saturday… usually going out… then like maybe a glass of wine during the week,” supporting that most drinking is on weekends.
When asked if she smokes: “I try not to smoke, but I do occasionally,” confirming occasional smoking.
In response to drugs: “I try not to smoke, but I do occasionally, but I don't take them,” indicating no drug use.
Living situation and support: “I live with my parents… I have a good support system. Like, I do have a good family and stuff,” confirming she lives with parents and has good family support.

She reports, “I talked to my mum because she also suffers from, or she's suffered from like depression in the past… I did talk to my mom about [it],” confirming discussion with a mother who has a history of depression.

Therapy: Doctor asks, “would you be happy to have some one to one therapy?” Patient: “Yeah, yeah, I think so. I've never done that before,” indicating she is open to therapy and has not had prior treatment.
The transcript contains only history; there is no mention of physical examination findings, supporting that no objective physical exam findings are documented.

Doctor frames it as anxiety related to work: suggests talking therapy “where they can really look at your situation, how you're reacting to what's provoking the anxiety,” and says palpitations are “most likely to be associated with anxiety.” Insomnia is prominent in the history. This supports an assessment of work-related anxiety with somatic symptoms (palpitations, insomnia).

Sleep disturbance is clearly secondary to anxiety about work: difficulty sleeping due to worry about work and racing heart; doctor notes “helping with your sleep patterns” in the context of anxiety management, consistent with secondary sleep disturbance due to anxiety.

Patient reports low mood and anhedonia (“I'm pretty much down… anything that previously was really fun is just not enjoyable”) but explicitly denies suicidality (“I haven't had any suicidal thoughts…”) and continues functioning at work, aligning with low mood/anhedonia without major depression or suicidality.

Doctor states: “it's probably worth having a couple of basic blood tests just to make sure that there's not something triggering [palpitations] off,” confirming basic blood tests to exclude physiological causes.

Doctor: “you can self refer via the NHS for what we call like talking therapy, which is a type of behavioral therapy… I can send you the link for that,” consistent with self-referral to NHS talking therapies (CBT-type) for anxiety.

Doctor mentions “there are some online resources that are really helpful… and I'll put some more information on your notes about helping with your sleep patterns and things like that,” supporting provision of online anxiety and sleep resources.

Doctor: “then arranging a GP follow up a week after you've had the test so we can just go through the results with you,” consistent with GP follow-up after blood tests to reassess and consider further management.

Doctor advises: “if you're feeling like it's not helping at all or your anxiety is getting worse to the point where you can't cope with work or you can't just do your normal things day to day, then it's important for you to give us a call back,” which matches advice to contact the service if symptoms worsen or functional impairment increases.
Follow-up plan: “arranging a GP follow up a week after you've had the test so we can just go through the results with you,” supports this follow-up statement.
